Back-related disability (Roland-Morris) in primary-care patients with sciatica

Dataset 2: Sciatica in primary care

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

Sciatica – leg pain radiating from the back along a nerve-root distribution – is one of the commonest reasons adults consult primary care for back trouble, and the practical question at that first consultation is not usually what is on the scan but how disabled is this patient and why. These data come from a cross-sectional diagnostic-accuracy study of 395 adults who presented to Dutch general practices with a new episode of sciatica and who underwent a standardised history, physical examination and lumbar MRI (Verwoerd et al.; sciatica in general practice, MRI substudy). Back-related disability is measured with the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ), the standard functional outcome in back-pain research, and it drives decisions about sick leave, physiotherapy referral and imaging.

Aim. Among primary-care patients presenting with sciatica, we examined which of age, sex, body mass index, back-pain intensity, leg-pain intensity, self-rated general health, comorbidity count and a positive neural-tension test are independently associated with the Roland-Morris disability score, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. Cross-sectional baseline data from a primary-care sciatica cohort: 395 adults consulting Dutch general practitioners with a new episode of sciatica, each assessed at a single occasion with a structured symptom questionnaire, a physical examination and a lumbar MRI. Age ranged from 19 to 82 years.

Variables. The outcome is disability_score, the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire total, an integer count of 0-23 endorsed disability items where higher means worse back-related function. Predictors are age_yrs (years), sex (reference: female, the larger group), bmi (kg/m²), back_pain_intensity (0-10 numerical rating scale), leg_pain_intensity (0-10 numerical rating scale), general_health (self-rated; reference: good, the largest group), comorbidities (reference: none, the largest group) and neural_tension_positive (at least one positive neural-tension test on examination; reference: no).

id is a participant label and is excluded from every model. clinician_sciatica – the GP’s high-confidence diagnosis of sciatica – is present in the file but is not used here. It is a clinician’s summary judgement formed from the very examination findings that are candidate predictors: it correlates 0.61 with neural_tension_positive, 0.54 with below_knee_pain and 0.49 with neurological_deficit. Entering it alongside those signs would put a variable and a summary of that variable in the same model, which makes the individual sign coefficients uninterpretable rather than merely imprecise. The remaining clinical signs (cough_sneeze_positive, below_knee_pain, subjective_sensory_changes, neurological_deficit) are omitted from the main model to keep it to eight predictors; neural_tension_positive is retained because it is the only examination finding with a clear crude association with disability (r = 0.22).

Statistical analysis. Linear regression (lm()), justified because the outcome is a 24-point score that is close to symmetric and spread across essentially its whole range, so a continuous approximation is reasonable. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(), supported by formal tests of heteroscedasticity, residual normality and collinearity; had non-constant variance been detected we would have reported HC3 robust standard errors via lmtest::coeftest() with sandwich::vcovHC(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 393 of 395 rows were analysed (2 dropped, 0.5%). Missingness in this file is small but real and confined to three columns: leg_pain_duration (19), bmi (2), back_pain_duration (2). The outcome itself is complete. Only bmi (2 missing) is in this model, so the loss here is trivial; a model containing leg_pain_duration would instead lose 19 further rows.

The sample is middle-aged (median 50 years), 60% female and overweight on average (median BMI 28.4 kg/m²). Symptoms are moderate to severe: median back-pain and leg-pain intensities are both near 6/10 and the median RMDQ score is 13 of 23, so half the sample reports disability on more than half the questionnaire items. Most rate their general health as good, and only 7 rate it poor – a sparse cell that will matter for that coefficient.

Exploratory figure

Figure 1. Roland-Morris disability score against back-pain intensity, split by self-rated general health. Lines are linear smooths with 95% confidence bands; points are jittered because both variables are recorded on discrete scales.

Disability rises steadily with back-pain intensity in every general-health stratum, and the “fair” and “poor” panels sit higher on the y-axis at the same pain level, which is the pattern a common-slope model with a general-health intercept shift is designed to capture; the “poor” panel contains only 7 patients, so its slope should not be read seriously.

Back-pain intensity is the strongest crude predictor: each additional point on the 0-10 back-pain scale is associated with a 1.21-point higher Roland-Morris score (95% CI 0.98 to 1.44, p < 0.001), so the difference between a patient reporting 3/10 and one reporting 8/10 is about 6.1 RMDQ points – roughly a quarter of the whole scale. Leg-pain intensity runs almost as strongly (1.03 points per NRS point, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.24). BMI is associated with higher disability (0.19 points per kg/m², 95% CI 0.1 to 0.28), patients rating their health as fair score about 2.8 points worse than those rating it good, and a positive neural-tension test carries roughly 2.3 points of extra disability. Age runs slightly the other way – older patients report a little less back-related disability – and sex and comorbidity count show no crude association.

Why adjustment is needed

The crude estimates above cannot be read as independent contributions because the symptom variables in this file travel together. back_pain_intensity is the clearest confounder of the leg-pain association: it correlates r = 0.61 with leg_pain_intensity and r = 0.46 with disability, so a patient with severe leg pain usually also has severe back pain, and the crude leg-pain slope is partly a back-pain slope in disguise. The Roland-Morris questionnaire asks about activities limited “because of my back”, which makes back pain the more direct cause of the score and leg pain the correlate. general_health is a second confounder: patients who rate their general health as fair or poor report higher pain intensities (mean back pain 5.7 versus 5.5 in those rating it good) and higher disability, so part of the crude pain effect is general ill-health rather than the sciatic episode. age_yrs is a third: age is associated with higher BMI (r = 0.1) and with comorbidity count, both of which are plausibly linked to function, so the crude negative age slope and the crude BMI slope each contain some of the other. Adjustment here is what turns “patients with worse leg pain are more disabled” into “at the same level of back pain, general health and body size, patients with worse leg pain are more disabled” – a much more defensible claim.

Adjusting for all eight predictors, back-pain intensity remains the dominant association: conditional on age, sex, BMI, leg pain, general health, comorbidity and neural tension, each extra point of back pain is associated with a 0.83-point higher RMDQ score (95% CI 0.54 to 1.12, p < 0.001). Leg-pain intensity stays independently associated at about half that size (0.45 points per NRS point, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.71, p < 0.001), so the two pain sites contribute separately rather than one standing in for the other. BMI keeps a clear independent association (0.14 points per kg/m², p < 0.001): a 10 kg/m² difference in body mass index corresponds to about 1.4 RMDQ points. A positive neural-tension test adds 1.5 points (p = 0.004), and rating general health as fair rather than good adds 2.26 points (p < 0.001). Age becomes more clearly protective once pain and body size are held constant (-0.052 points per year, p = 0.007), which over the 40-year age span here is around 2.1 points. Sex and comorbidity count contribute nothing. The model explains R² = 0.33 of the variance (adjusted R² = 0.312) with 35.7 observations per estimated parameter – comfortable for a linear model of this size.

Three estimates move meaningfully. Leg-pain intensity almost halves, from 1.03 crude to 0.45 adjusted – a move toward the null of about 57% – because back-pain intensity is now held constant; the crude leg-pain slope was substantially carrying back pain with it. It keeps its significance, so leg pain is not only a proxy. Fair general health attenuates from 2.73 to 2.26 points, again toward the null: much of the disability gap between patients who rate their health as fair and good is explained by their higher pain scores. The neural-tension test shrinks from 2.54 to 1.5 points but stays significant. Moving in the opposite direction, age strengthens away from the null (-0.042 to -0.052 per year) and goes from p = 0.044 crude to p = 0.007 adjusted – a mild suppression effect: older patients here have higher BMI and more comorbidity, which push disability up and were masking the downward age gradient. BMI barely moves (0.19 to 0.14) and neither does back-pain intensity (1.21 to 0.83), which tells us those two are not standing in for the rest of the variable set. Nothing loses significance on adjustment; only age gains it.

Diagnostics

Linearity. The fitted-versus-residual smooth is close to flat across the fitted range, and the posterior-predictive panel shows simulated data tracking the observed RMDQ distribution apart from a small pile-up at the scale ends – expected for a bounded 0-23 count.

Homoscedasticity. Constant variance is not rejected (check_heteroscedasticity() p = 0.449), so ordinary least-squares standard errors are reported as they stand and no HC3 re-estimation was required.

HC3 standard errors are within a few percent of the model-based ones for every coefficient except general_healthPoor, whose robust SE is roughly 1.7 times larger – unsurprising with only 7 patients in that cell. No conclusion changes, so the constant-variance assumption is doing no harm here.

Normality of residuals. Not rejected (check_normality() p = 0.116); the Q-Q plot is close to the reference line with mild thinning at both tails, which is what a bounded score produces.

Influential points. check_outliers() flags 0 observation(s) at the Cook’s-distance threshold, so no single patient is driving the fit.

Collinearity. All variance inflation factors are low; the largest is leg_pain_intensity at 1.88, far below the conventional concern threshold of 5. The two pain-intensity variables are correlated (r = 0.61) but not enough to destabilise their coefficients. This is the payoff of leaving clinician_sciatica out: a model containing it alongside the examination signs would have a substantially inflated VIF for neural_tension_positive, and including it here would have been indefensible.

Discussion

Among primary-care patients presenting with sciatica, back-related disability is driven mainly by how much pain the patient reports, not by what the examination finds. Back-pain intensity and, to a lesser but still independent extent, leg-pain intensity account for most of the explained variance; higher BMI and a positive neural-tension test add modest independent increments, poorer self-rated general health adds a further intercept shift, and older patients report slightly less back-related disability once those are held constant. Practically, a GP who wants to know how disabled a sciatica patient is should ask about pain intensity and general health rather than rely on the neurological examination – and should not expect the answer to be very predictable, since 67% of the variance in RMDQ score is left unexplained by all eight predictors.

Limitations. The design is cross-sectional and every variable was recorded at the same consultation, so nothing here separates cause from consequence: a patient who cannot do their usual activities may well report higher pain because of that, rather than the reverse. disability_score, back_pain_intensity, leg_pain_intensity and general_health are all self-reported on the same occasion by the same person, so common-method bias inflates their associations and the R² of 0.33 is an optimistic ceiling. The RMDQ is a bounded 0-23 count with visible mass at both ends (5 patients scored 0 and 6 scored 23), so a linear model necessarily allows fitted values outside the achievable range for extreme covariate patterns; a count or beta-binomial model would respect the bounds, at the cost of interpretability. The Poor general-health category has only 7 patients, so its coefficient is essentially uninformative and its wide confidence interval should not be read as evidence of no effect. The file contains no measure of psychological distress, fear-avoidance beliefs or work status, all of which are established drivers of back-related disability, so residual confounding is likely. Complete-case analysis dropped only 2 rows here, but the same predictor set plus leg_pain_duration would drop 19 more. All estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Future work. Repeating the RMDQ at three months would show whether baseline pain intensity predicts recovery of function rather than merely correlating with concurrent function.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Works well – this is the strongest of the three outcomes in this dataset. disability_score has zero missing values, spans its entire 0-23 range with a near-symmetric distribution, and yields R² = 0.33 with a genuinely mixed result set (four clearly significant predictors, two clearly null, one borderline). Good Purpose 3 teaching material.
  • Complete-case N = 393 of 395 (2 dropped, 0.5%), lost only to bmi. Adding leg_pain_duration costs 19 more rows for no gain – worth using as a demonstration of listwise deletion, not as a modelling choice.
  • No diagnostic failures. Homoscedasticity p = 0.449, normality p = 0.116, 0 influential points, max VIF 1.88. Unusually clean; students will not get to practise fixing anything here. HC3 SEs are shown anyway and are indistinguishable from OLS.
  • The clinician_sciatica trap is live. It is a column in the file, it is not an outcome, and it correlates 0.61 / 0.54 / 0.49 with neural_tension_positive, below_knee_pain and neurological_deficit. Students who throw every column into the model will include it. It is excluded here on interpretability grounds, not because the VIF is catastrophic – which is exactly the point worth teaching.
  • Sparse cell: general_health == "Poor" has 7 patients (7 in the full file). Expect a huge confidence interval on that coefficient. Collapsing to good vs fair-or-poor is a defensible student decision.
  • Bounded discrete outcome. 0-23 integers with 5 floor and 6 ceiling observations. The linear model survives the diagnostics but is formally the wrong support; do not let strong students be told the fit is “correct”, only that it is adequate.
  • Suppression on age (crude p = 0.044 to adjusted p = 0.007, moving away from the null) is a nice discussion point but reliably confuses weaker students.
